cards.title: Interactive compression with logarithmic input-length overhead
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal:
Is there an absolute constant \(K\in\mathbb R,\ K\ge1\) such that every two-party protocol \(\pi\) on \(n\)-bit inputs, under every joint input distribution \(\mu\), has a simulation \(\rho\) with distributional error at most \(1/100\) and worst-case communication at most
\[
K\bigl(I_{\mu}(\pi)+1\bigr)\bigl\lceil\log_2(n+2)\bigr\rceil\quad\text{bits}?
\]
Here \(n\ge1\), the protocol and simulation model, internal information cost \(I_{\mu}\), and joint-transcript error are defined below. There is no restriction on the finite communication cost of \(\pi\), and \(K\) must be independent of \(n,\mu,\pi\).

This is an explicitly selected editorial version of the source's proposed logarithmic-loss question. The source's surrounding paragraph concerns two-party internal information, despite the article's multiparty title. It already reports that compression without an overhead is impossible. The particular logarithmic factor, constant error, additive regularization and worst-case transcript-simulation guarantee below are specified here rather than attributed verbatim to its informal sentence.

source_formulation.text: Put differently, is it always possible to compress the communication cost of a protocol to its information cost?
source_formulation.caption: Complete selected source sentence; PDF p. 2

cards.why: The question asks how much communication is forced by interaction beyond the information actually transferred. A general small-overhead simulation would strengthen the connection between information-theoretic lower bounds and communication complexity, with consequences for direct-sum phenomena. A matching obstruction would show why correlated inputs prevent a near-information-cost account of interactive communication.
cards.status_note: The 2016 source and its expanded version explicitly leave a small-loss two-party compression direction open while acknowledging the failure of no-loss compression. This card spells out a particular logarithmic-input-length, internal-information, joint-transcript simulation variant. Because the source does not uniquely select all of those conventions, the exact editorial combination is labeled uncertain rather than represented as a verbatim source conjecture. The dated later-result checks and explicit editorial scope decision are recorded in the individual audit; no exhaustive current-status certificate or Lean verification is claimed.

cards.definitions:
Alice has \(x\in\{0,1\}^{n}\), Bob has \(y\in\{0,1\}^{n}\), and the pair \((X,Y)\) has an arbitrary probability distribution \(\mu\) on this finite product. The inputs may be correlated. Both parties know \(n\), the description of \(\pi\) and \(\mu\). Neither party is initially given the other party's realized input. No promise is placed on the support of \(\mu\).

A protocol uses one finite string \(R\) of shared fair random bits and two finite strings \(R_A,R_B\) of private fair random bits. The three strings are mutually independent and independent of \((X,Y)\). Their finite lengths may depend on the protocol and are not charged as communication. A length of zero is allowed. For each fixed public string, the protocol is a finite rooted binary communication tree: every internal node designates Alice or Bob, and the selected player sends one bit determined by their own input, private string, public string and the earlier messages. That bit selects the next child. A leaf terminates communication. The owner of the next message and termination are therefore determined by the public string and common message history, rather than by an uncharged timing channel. The transcript of communicated bits is \(M\), and the augmented transcript is \(T=(R,M)\). Both parties observe every communicated bit. A protocol is defined on every input pair and every coin choice. Its worst-case communication \(\operatorname{CC}(\pi)\) is the maximum number of transmitted bits over all these executions; it is finite but may be arbitrarily large.

All local computation, protocol descriptions and shared randomness are free. There is no restriction on the number of rounds or the local running time, and no privacy requirement. No advice depending on the other party's realized private input or quantum resources are supplied; all initial resources are exactly those specified above. Protocols for different \(n,\mu,\pi\) may be unrelated. This is an existence statement about finite communication protocols, not an efficient compiler for producing one from a table of \(\mu\).

For a finite random variable \(U\), its base-two Shannon entropy is
\[
H(U)=-\sum_{u}\Pr[U=u]\log_2\Pr[U=u],
\]
where \(0\log_2 0=0\). Conditional entropy \(H(U\mid V)\) is the average of \(H(U\mid V=v)\) weighted by \(\Pr[V=v]\), with zero-probability terms omitted. The conditional mutual information is
\[
I(U;W\mid V)=H(U\mid V)-H(U\mid V,W).
\]
The internal information cost in bits is
\[
I_{\mu}(\pi)=I(X;T\mid Y)+I(Y;T\mid X).
\]
All variables use the joint law of \(\mu\) and the three independent coin strings of \(\pi\). Including \(R\) in \(T\) accounts for public randomness; private coins are not included in that transcript. This is internal information, not the external quantity \(I(X,Y;T)\), and not the distinct multiparty public-information measure introduced in the source. The quantity is finite, nonnegative and at most \(2n\).

A simulation \(\rho\) is another finite protocol in the same model, with its own independent shared and private fair coins. At its terminal leaf Alice outputs a value \(T_A\) determined by her local view and Bob outputs \(T_B\) determined by his. These values lie in the finite set of augmented transcripts possible for \(\pi\), together with a failure symbol \(\bot\). Output descriptions and their lengths are not communication costs. The simulated public string of \(\pi\) is part of these output values; it need not equal \(\rho\)'s actual public string.

Let \(P\) be the law of \((X,Y,T,T)\) produced by drawing \((X,Y)\sim\mu\) and executing \(\pi\). Let \(Q\) be the law of \((X,Y,T_A,T_B)\) produced by drawing the same input distribution and executing \(\rho\). Regard both as distributions on the same finite product space, assigning zero mass to impossible original outcomes and to original failures. The simulation error is their total variation distance
\[
\operatorname{err}_{\mu}(\rho,\pi)=
\frac12\sum_{x,y,t_a,t_b}|P(x,y,t_a,t_b)-Q(x,y,t_a,t_b)|.
\]
Thus the requirement preserves correlation with the inputs and agreement between the parties' reconstructed transcripts, except for total variation at most \(1/100\). It is stronger than reproducing only an output bit of a particular function or only the unconditioned marginal law of \(T\). Error is averaged under \(\mu\) and the coins, whereas communication is worst case over every input pair and every coin string, including pairs of \(\mu\)-probability zero. There is no joint simulation of many independent copies. The \(+1\) in the cost bound avoids a zero-information boundary convention, and the logarithm is of the input bit length \(n\), not the number of possible inputs, the transcript length or the number of rounds.
cards.answer_criterion:
Provide a complete, mathematically correct Lean proof of the universal compression statement or its full negation. Equivalently, a positive answer gives one absolute constant \(K\in\mathbb R,\ K\ge1\) and proves
\[
\forall n\ge1\ \forall\mu\ \forall\pi\ \exists\rho:\quad
\operatorname{err}_{\mu}(\rho,\pi)\le\frac1{100}
\ \land\
\operatorname{CC}(\rho)\le
K(I_{\mu}(\pi)+1)\lceil\log_2(n+2)\rceil.
\]
A negative answer must prove that for every proposed \(K\in\mathbb R,\ K\ge1\), there are \(n,\mu,\pi\) in the stated domain for which every simulation with error at most \(1/100\) has communication strictly larger than that bound. A positive theorem only for product input distributions or public-coin original protocols does not cover the universal domain, although a matching lower bound within either subclass can refute the universal statement. Refuting only constant-overhead compression does not refute the logarithmic allowance. An expected-communication upper bound must be converted to the specified worst-case guarantee; error slack and an increased absolute constant can permit such a conversion. A theorem for external or multiparty public information must establish the claimed conclusion for the internal-information measure defined here to qualify. Likewise, failure of one simulation construction is not a lower bound for all simulations. The chosen constant simulation error is part of the mathematical proposition; the benchmark asks for a proof of that proposition or negation, rather than an approximate numerical verdict.

context_blocks.text: Interactive information measures what two participants learn about each other’s inputs during a conversation. The number of transmitted bits can be much larger. The source asks whether most of that discrepancy can always be removed while retaining the relevant behavior.

Reading the complete source paragraph changes the interpretation of the imported excerpt. It discusses the two-party question and says that compression with no loss is already ruled out. The open direction permits a small loss, giving logarithmic input-size dependence as an example.

The paper subsequently introduces a different public-information measure for multiparty computation and proves a compression theorem for it with logarithmic factors. That theorem cannot be substituted for a solution to the preceding two-party internal-information question.

Internal simulation reconstructs the original transcript for both participants while retaining its joint distribution with their inputs. The survey explicitly distinguishes this stronger requirement from merely computing the same total Boolean function. This card selects the transcript-simulation version.

Known exponential separations rule out compression solely to a fixed constant times information in general. Such statements must be compared with input size before treating them as a refutation of a logarithmic-input-length allowance.

Product-distribution compression assumes independent inputs. Compression to external information uses another information measure. These important positive results concern different domains or benchmarks from the present arbitrary-distribution internal target.

cards.title: Polynomial relation between classical and quantum communication
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Are randomized classical and entanglement-assisted quantum communication polynomially related for every total Boolean function? Precisely, do universal constants \(C\ge1\) and integer \(k\ge1\) exist such that \[R^{\mathrm{cc}}_{1/3}(F)\le C\bigl(Q^{\mathrm{cc},*}_{1/3}(F)+1\bigr)^k\] for every pair of nonempty finite sets \(X,Y\) and every function \(F:X\times Y\to\{0,1\}\)?
cards.why: The problem delineates quantum advantage in a basic distributed model with unrestricted local computation.

progress.text: The revised AND-functions paper proves the restricted \(O((Q^{\mathrm{cc},*})^7\log^2 n)\) deterministic bound while explicitly retaining the general Log-Equivalence Conjecture.
Hasegawa–Le Gall report polynomial separations using constant-round quantum communication. The claimed advantage does not exceed every polynomial.

Gavinsky posts a claimed exponential quantum–classical separation for an explicit total Boolean family, using two quantum messages and no prior entanglement. This matching claim was missed by the previous bounded status check.

Le Gall posts stronger claimed total-function separations and explicitly specifies public randomness, worst-case communication and per-input error. Pending proof verification, these claims would refute the universal polynomial relation.

context_blocks.text: Communication complexity isolates the information that must cross between two parties who already have unlimited ability to process their own inputs. A quantum advantage in this setting is therefore a saving in transmitted information, rather than a faster local computation. The shared entanglement in the quantum model is a free, input-independent resource.

For a total function, every combination of an Alice input and a Bob input must be handled. Promise problems may omit difficult combinations, and relations may accept several different answers. These distinctions prevent the known much larger advantages for those models from automatically providing a counterexample here.

The polynomial has to be the same for all functions. Examples in which the classical cost is a fixed power of the quantum cost are compatible with the conjecture, even if that power exceeds two. The negation requires advantages that defeat every fixed polynomial bound.

Bhattacharya and coauthors state this as the Log-Equivalence Conjecture, attributed to Shi and Zhu. Their earlier 2026 paper explicitly retains the general total-function question and studies a restricted composed family.

For \(F(x,y)=f(x_1\land y_1,\ldots,x_n\land y_n)\), their revised Theorem 1.2 gives \(D^{\mathrm{cc}}(F)=O((Q^{\mathrm{cc},*}_{1/3}(F))^7\log^2 n)\), where \(D^{\mathrm{cc}}\) denotes exact deterministic communication. This restricted AND-composition result, with its additional input-length factor, differs from the universal polynomial in quantum cost alone.

Hasegawa and Le Gall’s August 2026 preprint obtains a polynomial quantum advantage for a total function using a constant number of quantum communication rounds. Its improvement concerns interaction: the size of the communication gap remains polynomial. It therefore does not refute the general polynomial-relation conjecture.

Resolving the conjecture would determine whether total Boolean communication imposes a general limit on quantum savings. The comparison permits arbitrary prior entanglement and unrestricted interaction, so such a limit would apply beyond particular algorithms or graph-like compositions.

Gavinsky's preliminary August 2026 preprint claims an explicit total-function family with quantum cost \(O(\log^3 N\log\log N)\) and randomized classical cost \(\Omega(N^{1/6}/\log^{7/3}N)\), where \(N\) is the input length of each party. The stated quantum protocol has two transmissions and no prior entanglement; the classical lower bound permits any number of rounds. Polynomial growth in \(N\) defeats every fixed power of its logarithm, so this would refute the displayed conjecture if the proof is correct.

Le Gall's preprint of 15 September 2026 claims \(\operatorname{polylog}(n)\) quantum communication and \(\widetilde\Omega(\sqrt n)\) randomized communication with two quantum messages, and \(\widetilde\Omega(n^{1-1/j})\) classical cost for every fixed integer \(j\ge2\) with a larger constant number of quantum messages. Section 2 explicitly uses public randomness, unrestricted classical rounds, worst-case message costs and error at most \(1/3\) per input. These are total Boolean functions, not promise problems or relations. The full proof has not been independently verified here.

The new claims also apply to the comparison with free prior entanglement: a protocol using no prior entanglement is admissible when that resource is permitted. A protocol whose final receiver is Alice can send its output bit to Bob, adding at most one to the communication cost without changing the error probability. These model correspondences establish a match to the stated target; they do not certify the new lower-bound arguments.

cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal polynomial bound or of its negation. A negative answer must show that for every \(C\ge1\) and integer \(k\ge1\), some finite total Boolean function satisfies \(R^{\mathrm{cc}}_{1/3}(F)>C(Q^{\mathrm{cc},*}_{1/3}(F)+1)^k\). A superpolynomial separating family can witness this; one fixed polynomial separation cannot. A bound with an extra input-length factor, a promise-problem or relation separation, or a comparison imposing a fixed round limit does not resolve the stated all-functions, unrestricted-round target.
cards.definitions: Alice receives \(x\in X\), Bob receives \(y\in Y\), and Bob must output \(F(x,y)\). A protocol is agreed in advance for the entire function \(F\). Local computation and storage are unrestricted and free; only communication is charged. The protocol may depend on \(F\), but its shared resources are independent of the actual inputs. In the classical model the parties exchange bits and may use shared public randomness and private randomness. In the quantum model they exchange qubits, may use arbitrary finite-dimensional local quantum operations and measurements, and may start with any finite-dimensional shared entangled state independent of \((x,y)\). There is no fixed upper bound on the amount of this prior entanglement; its preparation is not charged. Local quantum operations are completely positive trace-preserving maps, with measurement outcomes retained in local registers, and the final output is a two-outcome measurement at Bob. Classical bits sent by a quantum protocol count as transmitted qubits. Neither model receives free input-dependent advice or any communication through timing, message length, silence or postselection. One may use a fixed finite alternating schedule of transmissions, padding unused transmissions; local branches cannot signal through the schedule. Arbitrarily many rounds are allowed, with no input-length-dependent round restriction imposed by the question. The cost is the worst-case total number of bits or qubits transmitted, including all rounds and all randomness or measurement branches. In either model the output must equal \(F(x,y)\) with probability at least \(2/3\) on every pair \((x,y)\). The quantities \(R^{\mathrm{cc}}_{1/3}(F)\) and \(Q^{\mathrm{cc},*}_{1/3}(F)\) are the least costs among protocols with this guarantee. Total means that all of \(X\times Y\) is the correctness domain; no additional joint promise is allowed. The additive one in the polynomial handles zero-communication functions. The constants \(C,k\) must be independent of the function, the domains, any bit encoding of the inputs, and the amount of shared entanglement.

cards.context:
Communication complexity isolates the information that must cross between two parties who already have unlimited ability to process their own inputs. A quantum advantage in this setting is therefore a saving in transmitted information, rather than a faster local computation. The shared entanglement in the quantum model is a free, input-independent resource.

For a total function, every combination of an Alice input and a Bob input must be handled. Promise problems may omit difficult combinations, and relations may accept several different answers. These distinctions prevent the known much larger advantages for those models from automatically providing a counterexample here.

The polynomial has to be the same for all functions. Examples in which the classical cost is a fixed power of the quantum cost are compatible with the conjecture, even if that power exceeds two. The negation requires advantages that defeat every fixed polynomial bound.

Bhattacharya and coauthors state this as the Log-Equivalence Conjecture, attributed to Shi and Zhu. Their earlier 2026 paper explicitly retains the general total-function question and studies a restricted composed family.

For \(F(x,y)=f(x_1\land y_1,\ldots,x_n\land y_n)\), their revised Theorem 1.2 gives \(D^{\mathrm{cc}}(F)=O((Q^{\mathrm{cc},*}_{1/3}(F))^7\log^2 n)\), where \(D^{\mathrm{cc}}\) denotes exact deterministic communication. This restricted AND-composition result, with its additional input-length factor, differs from the universal polynomial in quantum cost alone.

Hasegawa and Le Gall’s August 2026 preprint obtains a polynomial quantum advantage for a total function using a constant number of quantum communication rounds. Its improvement concerns interaction: the size of the communication gap remains polynomial. It therefore does not refute the general polynomial-relation conjecture.

Resolving the conjecture would determine whether total Boolean communication imposes a general limit on quantum savings. The comparison permits arbitrary prior entanglement and unrestricted interaction, so such a limit would apply beyond particular algorithms or graph-like compositions.

Gavinsky's preliminary August 2026 preprint claims an explicit total-function family with quantum cost \(O(\log^3 N\log\log N)\) and randomized classical cost \(\Omega(N^{1/6}/\log^{7/3}N)\), where \(N\) is the input length of each party. The stated quantum protocol has two transmissions and no prior entanglement; the classical lower bound permits any number of rounds. Polynomial growth in \(N\) defeats every fixed power of its logarithm, so this would refute the displayed conjecture if the proof is correct.

Le Gall's preprint of 15 September 2026 claims \(\operatorname{polylog}(n)\) quantum communication and \(\widetilde\Omega(\sqrt n)\) randomized communication with two quantum messages, and \(\widetilde\Omega(n^{1-1/j})\) classical cost for every fixed integer \(j\ge2\) with a larger constant number of quantum messages. Section 2 explicitly uses public randomness, unrestricted classical rounds, worst-case message costs and error at most \(1/3\) per input. These are total Boolean functions, not promise problems or relations. The full proof has not been independently verified here.

The new claims also apply to the comparison with free prior entanglement: a protocol using no prior entanglement is admissible when that resource is permitted. A protocol whose final receiver is Alice can send its output bit to Bob, adding at most one to the communication cost without changing the error probability. These model correspondences establish a match to the stated target; they do not certify the new lower-bound arguments.

cards.title: Fourier Min-Entropy–Influence conjecture
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Does there exist a finite universal constant \(C>0\) such that, for every integer \(n\ge1\) and every Boolean function \(f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\{-1,1\}\), some set \(S\subseteq[n]\) satisfies \(\widehat f(S)^2\ge 2^{-C I(f)}\)? Here \(I(f)\) is total influence under the uniform distribution. Equivalently, the conjecture asserts \(H_\infty(f)\le C I(f)\), with Fourier min-entropy defined below. The same constant must work for every dimension and every function.
cards.why: Total influence measures how often individual bit changes alter an output, while Fourier min-entropy measures how weak even the strongest parity correlation can be. A universal relation would constrain all Boolean functions without representation or balance assumptions. Its distinction from full Fourier entropy matters: controlling a single coefficient asks for less than controlling the entire spectral information, yet retains a connection to fundamental influence inequalities.
cards.status_note: The unrestricted conjecture is explicit in the 2021 primary paper and is still treated as a conjecture in the checked July 2026 Li–Tang publication. Their reported constant lower bound and Han’s general bound do not settle existence of a finite universal FMEI constant. This bounded source review does not independently verify every later proof or certify an exhaustive literature search.

sentences: The FMEI conjecture says that every Boolean function has a parity whose squared Fourier correlation is exponentially large in minus its total influence.
Both influence and Fourier coefficients use the uniform distribution on the Boolean cube.
One universal constant must cover every dimension and truth table, including constant and unbalanced functions.
The conjecture is weaker than full Fourier entropy–influence and remains meaningful because of its connection to fundamental influence inequalities.
Recent constructions force the universal constant to be at least four, while leaving the existence of any finite constant unresolved.

cards.definitions: Write \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). For \(S\subseteq[n]\), define the parity \(\chi_S(x)=\prod_{j\in S}x_j\), with \(\chi_\varnothing(x)=1\), and the normalized Fourier coefficient \(\widehat f(S)=2^{-n}\sum_{x\in\{-1,1\}^n}f(x)\chi_S(x)\). Set \(p_f(S)=\widehat f(S)^2\); these nonnegative masses sum to one. Define \(H_\infty(f)=-\log_2\bigl(\max_{S\subseteq[n]}p_f(S)\bigr)\), measured in bits. The maximum is positive, so this logarithm is always defined, even if some coefficients vanish. If \(x^{\oplus j}\) is obtained by changing the sign of coordinate \(j\), define \(I_j(f)=2^{-n}|\{x\in\{-1,1\}^n:f(x)\ne f(x^{\oplus j})\}|\) and \(I(f)=\sum_{j=1}^n I_j(f)\). Equivalently \(I(f)=\sum_{S\subseteq[n]}|S|p_f(S)\). Quantification includes constant functions, for which \(I(f)=H_\infty(f)=0\), as well as unbalanced, nonmonotone and arbitrarily complex functions. The witnessing set may be empty and may depend on the entire function. There is no algorithmic requirement to find it. In particular, the target is the largest squared Fourier coefficient, not the entropy of the truth table, the largest individual coordinate influence, or the Shannon entropy \(H(f)=\sum_{S:p_f(S)>0}p_f(S)\log_2(1/p_f(S))\). Changing the base from two to the natural exponential only rescales the universal constant.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the stated universal-constant inequality or its negation. A positive answer must establish one finite \(C>0\) for every dimension and Boolean function, with the normalized Fourier distribution and uniform influences above. A negative answer must prove that for every \(C>0\) there exist \(n\ge1\) and a nonconstant Boolean function \(f\) with \(H_\infty(f)>C I(f)\). Disproving one proposed constant, checking finitely many truth tables, or establishing a bound with a dimension-dependent factor does not settle this existence question. Determining the smallest possible constant is not required.

cards.title: Multiparty Clique lower bounds in compression games
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Do there exist a constant \(\varepsilon>0\) and an integer round bound \(r(N)\to\infty\) such that every nonuniform, deterministic, polynomial-party \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\)-compression protocol family deciding Clique with at most \(r(N)\) rounds has cost \(\Omega(N^\varepsilon)\)? Here \(N\) is the graph’s number of vertices. In each round, Alice sends messages to independent computationally unrestricted Bobs, receives their replies, and eventually computes the answer herself with an \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) circuit. Cost is the sum over rounds of the maximum length of an Alice-to-Bob message in that round.

cards.why: This asks whether many unrestricted helpers can compensate for Alice’s constant-depth computation using short messages and an increasing number of interactions. The source connects a positive answer for Clique to a major nonuniform circuit lower bound. The unusual communication measure makes precise model recovery essential to that connection.

sentences: Alice sees a graph and a requested clique size, but her computation is limited to polynomial-size constant-depth Boolean circuits.
She can exchange messages with polynomially many unrestricted helpers, each of whom sees only its own conversation.
Alice must compute the correct final answer on every input.

cards.definitions: For each integer \(N\ge2\), the input consists of the \(\binom N2\) adjacency bits of a simple undirected graph \(G\) on \([N]\), listed in lexicographic order of pairs \(i<j\), followed by \(\ell=\lceil\log_2(N+1)\rceil\) bits encoding a nonnegative integer \(k\) in ordinary most-significant-bit-first binary. The input length is \(L_N=\binom N2+\ell\). Clique is 1 if \(0\le k\le N\) and some \(k\)-vertex set has every pair joined by an edge; it is 0 when \(k>N\). The empty set makes the answer 1 for \(k=0\). Alice receives all input bits, while \(b_N\ge1\) Bobs receive no input. A protocol has a fixed number \(R_N\le r(N)\) of rounds. In round \(t\), Alice simultaneously sends a fixed-length binary string \(a_{t,j}\) to each Bob \(j\). Each Bob replies with a fixed-length binary string \(z_{t,j}\). Message lengths and all strategies are fixed before the input is known; empty strings are permitted. Bob \(j\)’s reply is an arbitrary deterministic function of the sequence \(a_{1,j},\ldots,a_{t,j}\), with no computational restriction. Bobs cannot communicate with each other or observe other Bobs’ messages. Each message \(a_{t,j}\) is computed by a Boolean circuit using the original input and all messages in earlier completed rounds. After the final replies, an additional circuit at Alice computes the single output bit from the input and the complete transcript. All of Alice’s circuits use only AND and OR gates of arbitrary finite fan-in, unary NOT gates, and constants. There are constants \(d\in\mathbb N\), \(A>0\) and \(a\in\mathbb N\), fixed across \(N\) for the protocol family, such that every Alice circuit has depth at most \(d\), and the sum of their gate, wire, input and output counts, the number \(b_N\) of Bobs, and the total number of transmitted bits are each at most \(A(N+1)^a\). Reply bits are not charged to communication cost, but remain subject to these polynomial length bounds. Alice’s circuits and all Bob functions may depend arbitrarily on \(N\); no uniform construction is required. No player uses randomness. Correctness means the output equals Clique on every input of length \(L_N\). Define \(c_\Pi(N)=\sum_{t=1}^{R_N}\max_{1\le j\le b_N}|a_{t,j}|\). The target quantifiers are \(\exists\varepsilon>0\;\exists r:\mathbb N_{\ge2}\to\mathbb N_{\ge1}\) with \(r(N)\to\infty\) and \(r(N)\le\lceil\log_2(N+1)\rceil\), such that \(\forall\Pi\) in the specified model deciding Clique, \(\exists C_\Pi>0\;\exists N_\Pi\ge2\;\forall N\ge N_\Pi,\ c_\Pi(N)\ge C_\Pi N^\varepsilon\). The constants governing polynomial circuit size, constant depth and the number of parties are arbitrary and may depend on \(\Pi\), while \(\varepsilon,r\) are chosen before \(\Pi\).
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of the quantified lower-bound statement, or a complete Lean-checked proof of its logical negation. The affirmative proof must cover every polynomial-size constant-depth Alice family and every collection of unrestricted Bob strategies, for the stated growing round budget and some exponent independent of the protocol family. A fixed-round lower bound whose exponent tends to zero as the chosen round count grows does not establish the target. Bounds on the total sum of all parties’ message lengths, a single-Bob model, average-case correctness or a different function do not establish this Clique statement.

context_blocks.text: The selected sentence follows the source’s conjecture of a polynomial communication lower bound with a growing number of rounds. This card interprets it as the existence of one growing round budget and one positive exponent that work against every polynomial-size constant-depth protocol family, with the lower-bound constant and starting length allowed to depend on the family.

The source uses input-bit length \(n\). This statement fixes a standard graph-and-threshold encoding and uses vertex count \(N\), with \(L_N=\Theta(N^2)\); a fixed positive polynomial exponent remains a fixed positive polynomial exponent under this normalization. The growing budget is capped at \(\lceil\log_2(N+1)\rceil\): existence of a lower bound for any growing budget also entails it for a smaller growing budget. Aggregate polynomial circuit and transcript bounds agree with the source’s polynomial resources in this round range.

In the multiparty model, Alice computes the final answer. An unrestricted Bob does not act as a referee who receives everyone’s messages. The Bobs are independent helpers with access only to their respective conversations with Alice, and only messages from Alice contribute to the stated cost.

Corollary 5.6 states that every function in \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}/\mathrm{poly}\) has polynomial-party \(\mathrm{AC}^{0}\) compression games of cost \(n^{O(1/r)}\) for each fixed positive integer \(r\). Here \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}/\mathrm{poly}\) means Boolean functions computed by nonuniform polynomial-size, bounded-fan-in circuits of depth \(O(\log n)\).

The paper consequently identifies the conjectured Clique lower bound as sufficient to separate \(\mathrm{NP}\) from \(\mathrm{NC}^{1}/\mathrm{poly}\). Its Majority bounds have round-dependent exponents and do not establish the required fixed exponent for Clique with an unbounded round budget.

cards.definitions: A linear threshold function has \(f(x)=\operatorname{sign}(\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_{i} x_{i}- \theta )\) for some real weights \(w_{i}\) and threshold \(\theta\), with \(\operatorname{sign}(t)=1\) when \(t\ge 0\) and −1 otherwise. cards.definitions: \(\gamma _{n}\) is standard Gaussian probability measure, the law of X with independent \(N(0,1)\) coordinates. Central symmetry means \(K=- K\), with symmetry about the origin. Convexity means \(tx+(1- t)y\in K\) for \(x,y\in K\) and \(t\in [0,1]\). Write \(1_{K}\) for the indicator of K. The convex influence in a Euclidean unit direction v is \(Inf_{v}[K]=(1/\sqrt{2}) E[1_{K}(X)(1- \langle v,X\rangle ^{2})]\). This is nonnegative for centrally symmetric convex K. The orthogonal subspace is \(v\perp =\{y:\langle v,y\rangle =0\}\), and \(C+\mathbb{R} v=\{y+tv:y\in C,t\in \mathbb{R}\}\) is a cylinder whose membership depends only on the projection \(x- \langle v,x\rangle v\). The symmetric difference \(K\triangle \mathrm{L}\) consists of points in exactly one of K and L, so its Gaussian measure is the probability that their membership indicators disagree. Empty sets and the whole space are permitted. No lower or upper bound away from zero or one is imposed on \(\gamma _{n}(K)\), and no bound on total influence is assumed.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove a single modulus \(\tau\) tending to zero that bounds the Gaussian approximation error uniformly over the stated sets, dimensions and directions, or prove that no such modulus exists. Equivalently for a negative answer, exhibit a sequence with directional influence tending to zero while its Gaussian distance from every symmetric convex cylinder in that direction stays bounded below by a positive constant. A dimension-dependent modulus or a cylinder in some other direction does not suffice.

cards.definitions: A De Morgan formula on \(n\) variables is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node is AND or OR; each leaf is one literal \(x_i\) or \(\neg x_i\), \(i\in[n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\). Evaluation uses the usual Boolean operations. Repeated occurrences of the same literal count as separate leaves, and subtrees cannot be shared. The leaf size is the total number of leaves. Define \(L(f)\) as the minimum leaf size among formulas evaluating to \(f(x)\) on every \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\). Formulas need not be monotone, balanced, depth-bounded or uniformly constructible. Let \(A=f^{-1}(1)\) and \(B=f^{-1}(0)\), both nonempty because \(f\) is nonconstant. A rectangle is a nonempty Cartesian product \(U\times V\) with \(U\subseteq A\) and \(V\subseteq B\). It is coordinate-monochromatic if there are a coordinate \(i\in[n]\) and a bit \(b\in\{0,1\}\) such that \(u_i=b\) for every \(u\in U\) and \(v_i=1-b\) for every \(v\in V\). Equivalently, a single literal separates the two sides, with either orientation permitted. A partition is a finite collection of such rectangles whose union is all of \(A\times B\), with distinct rectangles pairwise disjoint as subsets of ordered pairs. Row sets may overlap across rectangles, and column sets may overlap, provided the products do not. Define \(\chi(f)\) as the minimum number of rectangles in any such partition; coordinate labels and the descriptions of the row and column sets have no additional cost. Every pair \(a\in A,b\in B\) differs in some coordinate, so a singleton partition exists and \(\chi(f)\ge1\) is finite. No recursive or protocol-tree condition is imposed on a partition. The statement quantifies \(\exists C,d\;\forall n\;\forall f\) with the domains above. Both measures are nonuniform finite mathematical minima; no algorithm converting a partition into a formula is required. Restricting to nonconstant functions removes the empty-rectangle convention for constants without changing the substantive comparison.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean-checked proof of a universal polynomial bound \(L(f)\le C\chi(f)^d\), or a complete Lean-checked proof that \(\forall C\ge1\;\forall d\in\mathbb N\;\exists n\ge1\;\exists f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\) nonconstant with \(L(f)>C\chi(f)^d\). Refuting one proposed exponent or giving a constant-factor gap is insufficient to refute all polynomial bounds. A result for arbitrary communication relations, overlapping covers, positively oriented monotone partitions or algebraic tilings does not automatically establish the target for the defined partitions of total Boolean functions.

sentences: The question concerns square real matrices with low rank and at least half their entries equal to zero.
It asks for a Cartesian block consisting entirely of zeros whose area is a square-root-exponential fraction of the whole matrix.
The constant in that guarantee must be the same for every matrix and dimension.
The rank is over the real numbers, and entries may have arbitrary signs and magnitudes.
Recent results establish related guarantees under additional entry restrictions, while the checked sources retain the general real-matrix question.

cards.definitions: The rank is the dimension over \(\mathbb R\) of the span of the columns. A zero entry means exact equality to zero. Apart from the zero-density condition, entries may be arbitrary real numbers of either sign and magnitude; there is no finite-alphabet or integrality assumption. A rectangle is a Cartesian product \(I\times J\) of row and column index sets, and its size is its number of entries \(|I||J|\). The sets need not be consecutive, equal, or of the same cardinality. This is an area guarantee, with no separate lower bound prescribed for each side. The exponential is the real exponential function and \(\sqrt r\) is the nonnegative square root. The same constant must work for all dimensions, ranks, entries and zero patterns. When \(r=0\), the entire matrix is zero and the displayed bound asks for the whole matrix. The target is an existence theorem about matrices, not an algorithm with a specified input representation or running time.
cards.answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal statement, or of its negation. A negative answer must establish that for every real \(C>0\) there exist \(n\ge1\) and an admissible real matrix of rank \(r\) such that every all-zero rectangle has area strictly below \(n^2\exp(-C\sqrt r)\). One finite example violating a chosen constant does not refute the conjecture. A result restricted to Boolean, nonnegative integer, bounded-entry or intersection matrices does not settle the stated arbitrary-real target. No numerical approximation of matrix entries or of a zero test substitutes for exact equality.

context_blocks.text: A matrix can have many zero entries without those entries forming a large Cartesian block. The question asks whether a small dimension of the column span forces such a block, and specifies how much of the matrix it must occupy.

The conjectured area fraction is \(\exp(-C\sqrt r)\). It depends only on rank, even when the number of rows and columns is much larger. The constant is uniform: allowing it to depend on the particular matrix would remove the quantitative content of the question.

Lovett posed this precise half-zero-density, real-matrix, rectangle-area version in the 2013 Dagstuhl report. That report also states that the square-root dependence in the exponent would be best possible. The present formulation keeps its area target rather than requiring a balanced square.

For Boolean communication matrices, a constant rectangle is a collection of input pairs on which the answer is fixed. Low-rank real matrices allow a much wider range of entry values, so a theorem for Boolean matrices alone does not cover this question.

Hunter, Milojević, Sudakov and Tomon retain a broader sparse-real-matrix conjecture as Conjecture 1.8: when at most an \(\varepsilon\) fraction of entries are nonzero, a zero square of side \(n\exp(-O(\sqrt{\varepsilon r}))\) is predicted. That additional density parameter and square-side target are useful context, not replacements for the fixed-density area statement here.

Their Theorem 1.12 proves a related bound for nonnegative matrices whose nonzero entries are at least one and whose average entry is at most one half. In particular it gives the desired rank dependence for Boolean matrices with at least half their entries zero. A density of zeros does not impose the required average-entry bound on an arbitrary real matrix, and arbitrary signed entries fall outside the theorem.

Their Theorem 1.10 also resolves a related cross-disjoint-set-family conjecture, with its exponent measured by the size of the ground set. This result does not identify the ground-set size with the real rank of every matrix. Sudakov’s 2025 Oberwolfach report continues to list the general sparse-real-matrix statement as Conjecture 5.

cards.title: Quadratic decision-tree bounds from block sensitivity
cards.area: Communication complexity and Boolean function analysis
cards.formal: Does there exist a universal constant \(C>0\) such that every total Boolean function \(f:\{0,1\}^n\to\{0,1\}\), for every integer \(n\ge1\), satisfies \[D(f)\le C\,\operatorname{bs}(f)^2?\] Here \(D(f)\) is deterministic worst-case bit-query complexity and \(\operatorname{bs}(f)\) is block sensitivity, with both measures defined below. sentences: The target is a universal quadratic upper bound on deterministic decision-tree depth in terms of block sensitivity.
A decision tree adaptively reads individual bits and must compute a total Boolean function correctly on every input.
Block sensitivity counts disjoint blocks whose separate flips all change the value at one common input.
The known general bound is cubic, while quadratic bounds hold for several restricted classes.
The proposed constant must work for every function and dimension, and recent results on tree size or counts of minimal blocks do not settle this depth question.

cards.definitions: A deterministic decision tree is a finite rooted binary tree. Each internal node is labeled by an input coordinate \(i\in[n]\), with its two outgoing edges labeled zero and one; each leaf is labeled by an output bit. On input \(x\), the tree queries the bit \(x_i\) at the current node and follows the matching edge until it reaches a leaf. It computes \(f\) if the reached leaf equals \(f(x)\) for every \(x\in\{0,1\}^n\). Its worst-case query cost is the maximum number of internal nodes visited on any input, and \(D(f)\) is the minimum such cost over all trees computing \(f\). Repeated coordinate queries are permitted and count again. A leaf-only tree has cost zero. The tree may be chosen separately for each known function, and its number of leaves or total nodes is not the measured resource. No efficient construction of the optimal tree from a truth table or circuit is required. For \(B\subseteq[n]\), let \(x^{\oplus B}\) denote the input obtained from \(x\) by flipping exactly the bits in \(B\). A nonempty block \(B\) is sensitive at \(x\) if \(f(x)\ne f(x^{\oplus B})\). Define \(\operatorname{bs}(f,x)\) as the largest number \(t\) of pairwise disjoint nonempty blocks \(B_1,\ldots,B_t\) that are each sensitive at this same input \(x\), and let \(\operatorname{bs}(f)=\max_x\operatorname{bs}(f,x)\). Each block is tested by flipping it alone from the common input, not by a cumulative sequence of flips. Blocks need not be singletons or have a specified size. This maximum disjoint collection is different from the number of all minimal sensitive blocks and from fractional block sensitivity. All total Boolean functions are included: monotonicity, symmetry, graph invariance, bounded alternation, balanced output and succinct circuit representation are not assumed. Constant functions have \(D(f)=\operatorname{bs}(f)=0\) and satisfy the proposed bound. Randomized and quantum queries are outside the definition of \(D(f)\).
cards.answer_criterion: Provide a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean of the universal quadratic inequality or of its negation. A positive answer must establish one finite \(C\) that works for every dimension and every total function. A negative answer must establish that for every \(C>0\) there exist \(n\ge1\) and a total nonconstant Boolean function \(f\) for which \(D(f)>C\,\operatorname{bs}(f)^2\). Thus disproving the coefficient-one inequality is insufficient unless the ratios \(D(f)/\operatorname{bs}(f)^2\) are unbounded. A result for a subclass, a bound on decision-tree size instead of depth, or a bound with a dimension-dependent factor does not meet the criterion. The smallest possible constant and an efficient tree-construction algorithm are not required.

context_blocks.text: Jukna’s early draft poses \(D(f)=O(\operatorname{bs}(f)^2)\) as Research Problem 14.10 after Corollary 14.9 gives the general cubic upper bound. This card retains that constant-factor universal inequality, rather than asking only whether some polynomial relation exists.

Chugh, Podder and Sanyal’s 2023 paper states that the known general upper bound is cubic and the widest known separation is quadratic. Their Question 1 keeps the unrestricted gap open. Polynomial equivalence among measures, including the sensitivity theorem, does not by itself fix this exponent.

Their Theorem 4 establishes the quadratic bound for zebra functions, defined by having the same number of output changes along every increasing path from the all-zero input to the all-one input. This includes monotone and symmetric functions but is a restriction on the truth table. Their Theorem 5 also gives the quadratic bound when the maximum number of such changes is bounded by a fixed constant.

Chakraborty and Gál’s February 2026 paper improves bounds for the number of minimal sensitive blocks, and obtains consequences for the total size of decision trees. Those quantities differ from both the maximum number of disjoint sensitive blocks and the worst-case query depth in the present target. Its stated results do not establish the unrestricted quadratic inequality here.

cards.definitions: A sign matrix \(A\in \{- 1,+1\}^{r\times s}\) has positive finite numbers r,s of rows and columns and has every entry specified. Its sign-rank rank±\((A)\) is the least \(D\ge 1\) for which there are unit vectors \(u_{1},\ldots ,u_{r},v_{1},\ldots ,v_{s}\in \mathbb{R}\)ᴰ with \(A_{ij}\langle u_{i},v_{j}\rangle >0\) for all i,j. Equivalently it is the minimum real rank of a matrix B satisfying \(A_{ij}B_{ij}>0\) entrywise; zero entries do not realize either sign. The margin \(m(A)\) is the supremum, over such unit-vector representations in all finite dimensions D, of \(\min _{i,j} A_{ij}\langle u_{i},v_{j}\rangle\). It lies in (0,1]. In optimizing margin, the representation dimension is unrestricted; the representation of least dimension need not maximize margin. The requested d may grow arbitrarily rapidly as \(\rho\) tends to zero, but for each fixed positive \(\rho\) it must bound all matrix sizes. Equivalently, one can use a finite nondecreasing bounding function \(\eta\):[\(1,\infty\))→\(\mathbb{N}\). This uniform bounded-margin interpretation is explicitly restated in the later source’s Open Problem 1.3. Matrices with missing or promise-restricted entries are excluded.
cards.answer_criterion: Prove a finite size-independent bound \(d(\rho )\) for every positive margin threshold \(\rho\), or prove there is a fixed \(\rho >0\) and a sequence of fully specified finite sign matrices with margins at least \(\rho\) and unbounded sign-ranks. No efficient procedure for producing the low-dimensional representation is required. Unbounded sign-rank with margins tending to zero, or only for partial matrices, does not refute the statement.

cards.definitions: For \(n\ge 1\) and \(S\subseteq [n]\), put \(\chi _{S}(x)=\prod _{i\in S}x_{i}\), with \(\chi _{\varnothing}=1\). The Fourier coefficient is \(\hat\{f\}(S)=2^{- n}\sum _{x\in \{- 1,1\}^{n}}f(x)\chi _{S}(x)\), so \(f=\sum _{S\subseteq [n]}\hat\{f\}(S)\chi _{S}\). The support is \(\operatorname{supp}(\hat\{f\})=\{S:\hat\{f\}(S)\ne 0\}\), and \(k(f)=|\operatorname{supp}(\hat\{f\})|\). It is at least one. Identify a subset S with its incidence vector in \(F_{2}^{n}\) and define \(r(f)=\dim _{F_{2}}\) span\(\{1_{S}:S\in \operatorname{supp}(\hat\{f\})\}\). The empty set contributes the zero vector; it may count towards k but never increases r. This rank is not a real linear-span dimension of functions. The limit \(r(f_{j})=\omega (\sqrt{k}(f_{j}))\) means that for every real \(M>0\), the ratio eventually exceeds M. No bound on \(n_{j}\) in terms of j, explicit construction algorithm, or computational efficiency is requested. The negation is the existence of a universal constant C such that \(r(f)\le C\sqrt{k}(f)\) for every n and every such f. Since \(r(f)\le k(f)\), unbounded ratios necessarily require unbounded sparsities.
cards.answer_criterion: A positive answer must prove the existence of functions with unbounded \(r(f)/\sqrt{k}(f)\), equivalently a sequence with the displayed limits. A negative answer must prove a universal constant-factor square-root bound for every Boolean function. A fixed larger constant, finitely many examples, or a bound retaining a growing logarithmic factor does not decide the question.
